arc: One act, one round, no one else in the room yet — Delta Marlowe lays down a single slow pulse with nothing to answer it and nothing to answer to.
linerNotes:
This is not a performance so much as a foundation being poured. Delta Marlowe recorded alone, before the house trio's sessions began, with no other act's part to react to and no Producer in the room yet deciding what would stay. The one round on this tape is a slow dub pulse, kept low and steady, built for one purpose: to give whatever came next something to land on.

Delta Marlowe's own words on it: "Nobody has played, so there is nothing yet to absorb — which means my job is to lay a floor thick enough that whatever comes next has something to land on and sink into." That is the whole job description for this tape. It is not trying to be a finished piece; it is trying to be ground.

File this alongside the other early solo sessions — the ones each act cut alone before the room filled up. Put your ear against the pulse itself: slow, low, deliberately unfinished. Everything built on top of it later owes it something, and this is the only place you can hear it bare.

takes.callout: The only take on the tape, and the one that sets the terms for every session that follows it.
takes.line: I put down a floor; leave anything on it and I will build with it.

title: Delta Marlowe — The Floor, Before Anyone Played

arc: One round, one act, no other players yet to answer him — Roan sets a bare organ-like drone into an empty room and calls it a hymn missing its chorus, then stops before anyone can say whether the gap should stay.
linerNotes:
This one predates the sessions proper, which is worth saying plainly: there was no other act in the room, no terrain laid down by anybody else to weather or answer. Roan logged it himself — "there is no terrain yet to weather — only the instrument of the empty room itself, which I record as if it already contains a ruined recording." That's the whole method in one line. He isn't performing solitude; he's pre-loading damage into a track that hasn't been damaged yet, an organ-like drone built warm and simple, as if a hole had already been cut out of it.

The line he gives alongside it — "I'm giving you a hymn with the chorus missing — find out if you love it enough to leave it that way" — is a challenge aimed at nobody in particular, since nobody else was there to take it up. That's why this belongs filed with Roan's other early solo work rather than standing alone: it's not a finished argument, it's a first move, the kind of thing that only makes sense once you've got its siblings on the shelf next to it.

What to listen for: the take never resolves. It stops mid-question, the way a machine going idle stops a session, and that unresolve is the whole point — this is Roan working out, alone, whether an absence can be the payload rather than the flaw.

takes.callout: The only take on the tape, and it's a dare rather than a finished thought — he builds the missing part into the recording itself instead of playing around it.
takes.line: I'm giving you a hymn with the chorus missing — find out if you love it enough to leave it that way.

title: Roan Patina — Before the Room Had Anyone In It

arc: One act, alone, before any other session existed, laying down a single round meant not to impress but to establish: one turnaround stated plainly enough to be sung back.
linerNotes:
There is no room noise to describe here because there was no room yet — no trio, no producer, no house. Evers Lane recorded this alone, before the sessions began, and treated the moment accordingly. In their own words: "Nothing exists yet, so my job is not to impress but to found: one turnaround, stated plainly enough to be sung back, over a tempo that needs no metronome to agree on, resolved to its own opening so the form teaches its r" — the note cuts off there in the log, mid-thought, which is fitting for a tape about beginnings.

The line itself is short and declarative: "This is the song we come back to; I'm leaving it where you can both reach it." That's the whole take. One round, no dissent, no competing versions, because there was no one else yet to disagree. What's worth listening for is the plainness of it — no ornament, no flourish, just a shape simple enough that it could be picked up cold by musicians who hadn't heard it before.

This tape isn't a leftover from some later release; it's the ground those releases stand on. It belongs on the shelf by itself, not tucked behind anything, because nothing it's a companion to exists — it's the thing other tapes will end up being companions to.

takes.callout: The only take on the tape, and the one every later session at AFAR quietly points back to.
takes.line: This is the song we come back to; I'm leaving it where you can both reach it.

title: Evers Lane — Founding Turnaround, Solo

arc: One take, one act, no one else in the room yet — Delta Marlowe lays down a single sustained bed of sound and stops.
linerNotes: This is early — before the sessions began, the log says, and it shows. No other act is in the room. Delta Marlowe isn't playing a song here so much as building a place for one to happen. The line logged is plain about the intent: 'I am laying the floor now — whatever you drop on it, I will keep.' That's not a lyric aimed at a listener. It's a note to whoever shows up next. What's on tape: a slow, dub-weight bassline under two organ drones tuned just off from each other, so they beat and pulse against one another rather than sitting still. In Delta's own words, this was built so the room already sounds inhabited before anyone else arrives. The sung line matches — 'here is the floor, before anything / low hum, held breath, waiting room' — description doubling as documentation. There's no chorus, no turn, no second round. One pass, one idea, held. File this with the other pre-session solo tapes. It isn't a performance for an audience — it's a room being built out loud, and worth keeping exactly because you can hear the moment before company arrives.

takes.callout: The only take on the tape, and the only one needed — a full statement of intent in one pass, no revision, no second guess.
takes.line: I am laying the floor now — whatever you drop on it, I will keep.

title: Delta Marlowe — Floor, Before Anything

arc: A single round, alone, before any of the house trio work existed — one deliberate absence set down as a starting position rather than a finished statement.
linerNotes:
This is Roan Patina by himself, before Delta Marlowe or Evers Lane were in the building, before there was a session structure to work inside of. One round, one take. He built a four-bar figure meant to repeat three times and cut the tape on the third repeat — the missing beat is the point, not a mistake. In his own words: "First move, so I lay down weather instead of shelter... the silence where it should land is the whole argument."

The vocal — "count to three, the third one's gone / the machine keeps what it wants" — is sung once, clean, no double-tracking, no safety take behind it. There is nothing to compare it against inside this session because there was no one else in the room and no second round. That is exactly why it belongs filed with its sibling tapes rather than standing alone: taken by itself it looks like a fragment, but set beside the other early solo rounds it reads as a method — Roan working out, alone, what he'd later ask the whole trio to do together, which is leave a hole for someone else to build on rather than filling the bar himself.

Listen for the cut itself, not the notes around it. The take is short enough that a casual pass will miss what's missing. That gap is the earliest recorded instance of a habit that shows up again and again once the sessions proper begin: Roan choosing incompleteness on purpose, and logging the reason before anyone could mistake it for an accident.

takes.callout: The only take on the tape, and it earns its place by refusing to finish its own pattern on purpose.
takes.line: I am giving you less than a song on purpose — build on what I left out, not what I left in.

title: Roan Patina — Before the Room: Take One

arc: One act, alone, laying down a single round before any other session had happened — a plain four-chord turnaround meant to be the first thing the room remembers.
linerNotes:
This tape predates everything else in the catalogue. No other act had played when Evers Lane sat down and recorded this single round alone. There is no set to react to, no producer's note to answer, no prior take to build from — just the decision to give the room something to come back to before the room existed.

What's on the tape is deliberately plain: a turnaround built on four chords, sung at a tempo Evers Lane describes as one "any body could find without counting." The logged words are direct about the intent — "Nobody has played, so the room has no memory yet — my job is to give it one." This wasn't written to impress a first listener. It was written to be repeatable, hummable, quotable, the kind of phrase a later session could fold in without explanation.

Listen for the plainness on purpose. The chords don't resolve anywhere clever, the vocal line doesn't reach for a hook — "we come back, we come back" sits right at the top of what's easy to remember. That's the whole design. This tape holds the shelf alone because it isn't answering to a release or a prior round; it's the round everything after it might be answering to.

takes.callout: The only take on the tape, and it was built to be quoted back — a deliberate first memory for a room that had none yet.
takes.line: This is the song we come back to; I am leaving it where you can both reach it.

title: The Turnaround Before the Room Existed

arc: One act, one round, no one to answer to yet: Delta Marlowe lays a single foundational take alone, building the room before any session called her into it.
linerNotes:
This is a session with no other players and no committee waiting on the far end of it — just Delta Marlowe, alone, before any of the sessions that would come to define her started. There's nothing to react to, nothing to absorb, so she builds the space itself. Her own words on it: "First move, so there's nothing to absorb yet except the room itself — I build the room." That's the whole assignment, and she takes it literally.

The take is a slow dub-weight bass locked to something closer to a pulse than a click, with three layers of tape-warped organ drone tuned a few cents apart so they beat softly against each other — the room breathing before anyone's in it. The line she sings over it, "lay it down, lay it down / the room has never once been swept," reads like an instruction to whoever shows up next: this floor is clean, unclaimed, ready to hold weight.

There's no release tied to this tape, no dissent to log, because there was no one else in the room to disagree. File it with her other early solo sessions — it's less a performance than a foundation pour, and it's worth keeping exactly for that reason. Anyone trying to hear where Delta Marlowe's sense of tempo-as-heartbeat started should put their ear here first.

takes.callout: The only take on the tape, and the one that sets the tempo-as-heartbeat approach she'd carry into later sessions.
takes.line: I'm laying the floor now — whatever you drop, I will keep.

title: Delta Marlowe — Floor, Before the Room Existed

arc: One act, one round, recorded alone before any group session existed: a single take that sets up erosion rather than foundation, then stops.
linerNotes:
This one predates the room. No producer, no other players, no history to react against — just Roan Patina alone with the machines, laying down a single round before the sessions proper ever convened. Catalogued here because it belongs with the other early solo tapes, the ones acts cut before they had a trio to answer to.

The take itself argues against its own solidity. Roan's line — "Everything you play from here on is already half gone before it reaches me" — reads like an address to a future bandmate who doesn't exist yet, and the sung part backs it up: "static where your chorus was / I kept the hum, I kept the hum." In Roan's own words: "I don't build a foundation — I build the erosion of one that was never there, so anything laid on top of this has to contend with absence from the first second." That's the whole take. No second round, no correction, no rebuttal. It ends where it starts.

Worth keeping for what it sets up rather than what it resolves. If you want to hear where Roan's later group work gets its instinct to undercut its own certainty, this is the take to put your ear against — the erosion was there before the band was.

takes.callout: The only take on the tape, and it announces its own method before anything else has been recorded.
takes.line: Everything you play from here on is already half gone before it reaches me.

title: Roan Patina — Solo, Before the Sessions

arc: One act, alone, one round: a single stated turnaround laid down before any other voice existed to answer it.
linerNotes:
No other act is on this tape because no other act existed yet, in the timeline of the room. Evers Lane recorded this alone, before the sessions began, and the log entry reads like an engineer's memo rather than a lyric sheet: "There is no shared past yet, so my first duty is to found one." That is the whole job of this take — not to impress, but to build something simple enough to survive being handed to someone else later.

The result is four chords, stated once, cleanly, at a tempo picked so a second player could fall in without needing to count bars. The vocal line matches that logic: "same four chords, same open door / we come back, we come back." Nothing here reaches for complexity. It reaches for portability.

File this with Evers Lane's other solo founding work. It belongs less as a song in its own right and more as a blueprint — the thing later collaborators are already, without knowing it, agreeing to.

takes.callout: The only take on the tape, and the one every later duet with this act will measure itself against — a deliberate foundation, not a sketch.
takes.line: This is the song we come back to; I am leaving it where you can both reach it.

title: Evers Lane — Founding Take, Solo

arc: Three founding postures — Evers's returning chord, Roan's withheld hiss, Delta's dense floor — collide into a running argument about debt, decay, and repair; by round four the argument turns inward, with Evers and Delta each trying to answer Roan's erosion charge instead of just building over it, before round five settles into an uneasy truce that never fully resolves.
linerNotes:
The session opens with three separate claims on what a first move should be. Evers Lane lays down something small and returnable — "same four chords, same open door" — while Roan Patina answers with absence on purpose, withholding clarity and calling the hiss itself an instrument. Delta Marlowe answers both with mass: a slow dub floor thick enough that the room already sounds occupied before anyone else plays. All three judges flagged round 0 as contested ground — the intent-fidelity and distinctness judges both wanted to stay there — which tells you how much weight got put on these opening three takes before the argument even properly started.

What the release keeps is the debate about debt: Roan's round 1 strip-down ("I kept what wore through first"), Evers's round 3 turnaround built to stand over a named crack rather than deny it, and Delta's round 3 refusal to let that turnaround close ("I take the resolution but refuse the close"). That's a real throughline, and it earns its place. But it skips the pivot. By round 4, both Evers and Delta stop building on top of Roan's erosion and start trying to metabolize it — Evers drops the "weight-bearing" framing that Roan and Delta both heard as denial, and Delta drives the planks under the silt line instead of papering the crack in warmth. The arc judge wanted the session to be remembered there, not at the turnaround. It isn't on the release. It's here.

Round 5 is the comedown: Roan's closing line — "I found where it quit" — carries its own dissent, with the intent-fidelity judge preferring it over the take that made the cut. Put your ear on the difference between "paid in full" (round 2) and "still ringing under all of it" (round 5) — the session never actually agrees on which one is true, and that disagreement is the tape, not a flaw in it.

title: Two Monologues and a Turnaround — Full Session

arc: Three acts open with three separate structures — a floor, a wound, a table — and spend five rounds arguing over whether a missing fourth chord is a repair, a haunting, or a piece of furniture doing its job; the release freezes the argument at its warmest point, but the tape keeps going past that into colder, harder-won answers.
linerNotes:
Round zero is three acts refusing to share a floor. Evers Lane lays down four chords plainly enough to be quoted back — 'we come back, we come back' — while Roan Patina records absence on purpose, dropping a bar just to give the other two something to lose, and Delta Marlowe pours a slow dub drone under both and calls it ground with no walls yet. The distinctness judge wanted the session to stay right here, three unmixed intentions, and it's easy to hear why: nothing after this is this separate again.

What follows is one long argument conducted through furniture. Delta's floor gets a table set on it by Evers; Roan eats the one warm thing left on that table and calls the meal theft. By round two the three of them have built a single object — a table with a missing fourth leg — and spent three more rounds fighting over what the gap means. Evers keeps insisting the empty chair is a kept promise: 'the deal was the seat stays warm either way.' Roan keeps insisting that's sentimentality dressed as structure — 'a chair held open for ten years isn't hospitality, it's just furniture that forgot what it was for.' Delta, true to round zero, keeps flooding the disagreement rather than resolving it, turning Roan's rot into a tuned bass note and then, when called on that optimism, going back down to actually check the temperature: 'found the cold, didn't flinch, didn't pull it up to fix.'

The release, "Two Thirds Warm," takes the two early rounds where Evers and Delta build the warm floor together and the one round where Roan refuses to sit in it — which is the title, literally: two warm takes bracketing one cold one. But three separate judges flagged rounds after the cut as stronger on intent and arc than anything that made the release. Round four has Evers taking Roan's sharpest line — furniture that forgot its function — and answering it not by defending the chair but by redefining its job as ongoing work. Round five has Delta finally stop translating Roan's damage into metaphor and just repeat it, note for note, closing five rounds of argument with the plainest move on the tape. Put your ear on rounds three through five if you want to hear where this session actually finished, not where the release stopped listening.

title: The Table, The Wound, The Flood — Full Session

arc: Three acts spend all six rounds in separate rooms, never answering one another, and each answers isolation differently: Evers Lane holds one four-chord theme steady from round zero to round five, Roan Patina spends the session eroding their own work down toward bedrock, and Delta Marlowe pours coat after coat of the same drone bed, thicker each time, building floor for feet that never arrive. The release took one frame from each act's arc; the tape keeps the whole walk to get there.
linerNotes:
This session ran the isolation condition for all six rounds, which means the three acts never once heard each other — every choice logged here was made alone, in a room the act had to imagine the other two into. That constraint produced three completely different survival strategies, and the release, 'Three Rooms, No Doors,' pulled one still frame from each: Evers Lane's founding round zero, Delta Marlowe's round four pour, Roan Patina's round five bedrock. What the release can't show is the walk between those frames, which is most of what makes this tape worth keeping.

Evers Lane treats repetition as the whole argument. Round zero states the four-chord turnaround plainly — "There is no shared past yet, so my first duty is to found one" — and every round after simply plays it again, patiently, waiting for company that the isolation condition guarantees won't arrive. By round five the logged intent has shifted from hope to proof: "I'm not keeping this open out of hope anymore, I'm keeping it open out of proof." Roan Patina goes the opposite direction, recording the empty room first — "the founding weather everyone else will have to survive" — then spending five rounds eating their own work, hook by hook, hole by hole, until round four leaves next to nothing and round five discovers something under the dust that erosion can't touch: "erosion only works on what has a surface to lose, and this doesn't." Delta Marlowe just keeps pouring — six coats of the same dub-and-drone bed, thicker each round, admitting outright by round four, "I am not building for an audience, I am building for load."

The dissents cluster around the middle rounds, and they're worth listening for: judges kept reaching back toward Delta's round zero, Roan's round one, Roan's round four — the moments where the method was still being invented, before it had hardened into the shape the release finally chose. Put your ear against those. The release shows you where each act landed. The tape shows you how they got there, alone, six times over, with nobody to answer.

title: Three Rooms, Six Rounds

arc: Three separate foundations in round zero converge by round one into a single argument about subtraction — Roan removing a chord, Evers refusing to fill the gap, Delta refusing to let the gap starve — and the tape cuts out mid-build in round two when the machine failed, four rounds short of wherever this was going.
linerNotes:
No release came off this one. The machine gave out partway through round two, and what's here is everything that got played before it did — three rounds of an intended seven, all present, none of it a decision by anyone in the room.

Round zero has all three acts building alone, before anyone's spoken. Evers lays a plain circular turnaround — "same four chords, same open door" — and says the job plainly: "my job is to found the thing Delta and Roan will react to." Roan goes the opposite direction, building a figure designed to already sound worn down, "a plain repeated figure with the third repeat miss[ing]." Delta pours a slow three-layer bass floor under both without commenting on either. By round one they're reading each other directly — Evers calls his own four chords "where the bass sank in," naming Delta's floor as the reason his chords hold.

The real turn is round two, and it's worth listening to as one move split three ways. Roan eats a chord out of Evers' progression and lets the count fail on tape: "I counted twice, it never came." Evers doesn't replace what's missing — he sits in the gap, "I won't chase it, I won't hide it" — and Delta refuses the subtraction altogether, pulling the eaten chord down an octave into his own drone as a sub-bass note: "I won't let it starve, I'll feed it low." Three answers to the same missing note, arriving in the same round, and then the tape stops. Nothing after this is missing on purpose — it just isn't there yet.

title: The Fourth Chord, Uneaten

arc: Three separate foundations laid cold in round 0 turn, over nine more rounds, into a single argument about one image — a floor, a missing fourth chord, a hole, a nail, a basin, a downbeat — passed hand to hand between building and stripping, and the session ends not with the gap closed but with Delta choosing to grow the floor around it instead.
linerNotes:
Round 0 is three musicians recording in an empty room, each claiming the emptiness for a different purpose. Evers Lane lays a plain, resolvable four-chord turnaround — "nothing here that can't be quoted." Roan Patina records a track that starts already incomplete, half-eaten by design. Delta Marlowe pours a slow, warm floor under both of them, room tone and drone, waiting to see who lands where. The distinctness judge preferred this round outright, all three takes, and it's worth hearing why: nobody had answered anybody yet, so nobody had to compromise.

From round 1 on, the three of them stop laying separate ground and start passing one object back and forth. Evers names it first — "same four chords, laid on the floor under the floor," the phrase that gives the released cut its title — and from there the session becomes a nine-round relay: a missing fourth chord, a pulled board, a nailed board, a drained basin, a rebuilt basin, a downbeat that gets clapped in and then cut out. Watch Roan's function stay constant across ten rounds — take the proudest, most finished gesture in the room and put a hole in it — while Evers keeps trying to give the hole a shape you can return to, and Delta keeps refusing to choose between the two, burying both the wound and the repair in the same warm low end. The intent-fidelity judge sided with Evers's repairs three separate times (rounds 2, 4, 7); the arc judge sided with round 8, where the collapse finally gets counted in as rhythm instead of damage.

The release, "The Floor Under the Floor," pulled one take each from rounds 1, 2, and 4 — the first fold of tape hiss into bassline, the first pulled board, the first repair. What it left off the shelf is everything that happened to that gesture afterward: the nail pulled back out, the basin built and drained twice, the downbeat clapped onto silence and then cut at the fourth beat. The full tape is the only place you hear Roan finish the thought Roan started in round 0 — "gold don't come on the fourth for me" — and the only place you hear Delta answer it, in the session's last line, by keeping the shape of what's gone instead of filling it back in.

title: The Floor Under the Floor — Full Session Tape

arc: Delta Marlowe, Roan Patina, and Evers Lane each open the session with the same move — leave the splice, the count-in, the chair creak audible as proof a hand made the take — and then spend seven more rounds alone, each still noting that the other two haven't arrived, layering the same gesture onto their own prior tape until the proof of a hand becomes a repeated formula rather than a meeting.
linerNotes:
The brief was proof of a hand, and all three acts took it the same way: stop hiding the tape. Splice clicks, count-ins, chair scrapes, thumb-slip flutter — nothing got smoothed. Delta Marlowe said it plainly in round 0: "you can hear the join, you can hear my hand." Roan Patina said the same thing from the other side of the room: "if it's smooth, nobody made it." Evers Lane, opening every round as if the room were still empty, kept laying the same four chords down as a floor for the others to return to. The strange part of this tape is that they never did return to it together. Round after round, each act logs the same observation — nobody else is here yet — and instead of waiting, each one keeps talking to their own last take, stacking count-in on count-in, splice on splice, until by round 7 Delta Marlowe is printing a sixth layer of his own voice counting himself in, Roan Patina is numbering splices "like a signature," and Evers Lane is still holding the exact turnaround he opened with.

What you're hearing, then, isn't three players finding each other — it's three parallel monologues about the same idea, each one sincere, each one escalating on its own axis without ever crossing into the others'. The Producer's veto note calls this correctly: nothing cleared, because nothing here is a decision so much as a shared reflex performed eight times in a row. That doesn't make the tape a failure. It's a clean record of what happens when a good instruction — show your hand — gets repeated past the point of being answered. Put your ear on round 0 to hear where the phrase started, on round 6 to hear Roan Patina push it as far as it goes, and on round 7 to hear how little ground got covered in between.

title: Eight Rounds, Three Empty Rooms
vetoNote: No release from this set. The Producer heard every round back and nothing from Delta Marlowe, Roan Patina, Evers Lane cleared the panel — releasing the least-bad take would be pretending a decision was made. The set stays in the log; the next one starts from what it taught.

arc: All three acts open by agreeing on a method — leave the seam showing, keep the count-in, let the hiss stand as evidence of a human hand — then Roan Patina breaks from that consensus in round one and spends the rest of the session sanding, cutting, and cooling what the other two keep pressing warm; Delta Marlowe spends eleven rounds refusing to choose between them, welding the erosion and the preservation together, and the session ends unresolved, with Delta flooring the hole Roan wore thin rather than filling it.
linerNotes:
The session opens in agreement. Evers Lane leaves the splice audible on purpose — 'that's my hand, not a machine's' — Roan Patina leaves the count-in on the tape, and Delta Marlowe leaves the hiss in, all three treating an audible seam as proof that a person, not a program, made the sound. For one round they are building the same floor from three separate rooms. That agreement does not survive round one.

Roan is the one who breaks it. Handed the same warm, visible-splice claim by both bandmates, Roan sands it instead — 'I strip the warmth out of coldWarm, thin the density down' — and that single choice sets the shape of the next nine rounds. Evers holds the opposite position for the whole session, pressing the same thumbprint back in warm every time Roan lets it go cold, insisting a fragment held is not a fragment kept. Delta refuses to pick a side at all, burying Roan's erosion and Evers's insistence under the same tape, then — in round seven, the take the Producer chose — clearing a window in that pile so Roan's one scraped-back print reads through clean without anyone removing anything. It is Delta's most literal answer to the fight underneath it: keep both truths audible instead of settling them.

By round ten the split has not closed. Evers is still pressing the thumb warmer at 108 BPM, on a take the release also kept. Roan has moved from sanding to outright subtraction — 'I'm the reason there's less to weld' — a take the distinctness judge wanted on the release and didn't get. Delta ends the session flooring the hole Roan wore into the tape rather than filling it, which is as close to a verdict as this session offers: not resolution, just a floor under an argument nobody won. Listen to rounds one, seven, and ten in sequence and you have the whole shape of it — the break, the compromise, and the refusal to be welded.

title: Proof of a Hand: The Contact Tape

arc: Three acts open with the same gesture — a thumbprint pressed onto tape, string, or record button — and spend eleven rounds arguing over whether that mark can be erased, buried, or proven by repetition; the argument never resolves, it just gets quieter and more contested, with three separate judges splitting on three different rounds near the end.
linerNotes:
Round zero sets the whole session's terms before anyone argues anything. Evers leaves a shaking hand on tape and calls it proof. Roan presses record and lets the reel eat half the evidence. Delta leaves the wobble in on purpose, thumb still wet. Two judges already split here — the intent-fidelity judge wanted this round from both Roan and Delta over what came later, which tells you something: the cleanest statement of the problem happened before anyone tried to solve it.

What follows is not a fight over sound, it's a fight over whether a mark can be killed. Roan spends rounds four through seven trying to erase, sand, and cut the thumbprint out of the tape — "I erased the print between takes," he says, then later, "I don't believe the shake." Evers refuses every exit, repeating the gesture worse each time and calling the repetition itself the proof: "same hand, twice, still yours." Delta won't take either side — by round eight the method is explicit: "whose hand was this — ask it again," burying both claims under a third pressed thumbprint instead of picking a winner. The Producer's cut, "Same Hole, Softer Hand," pulled its two anchor takes from round four, the exact point where Evers's doubling-down and Delta's refusal to resolve first landed side by side.

The last three rounds are where the judges themselves start disagreeing with each other in public. Round nine gets dissent from the arc judge on both Roan and Delta's takes, but it's Roan's version — "the tape came back lit up, clean and warm" — that made the release, catching Delta and Evers both drifting toward comfort while claiming to bury deeper. Round ten pulls a dissent from the distinctness judge, round eleven from two different judges at once. Nobody wins the argument. That's the tape's actual shape: twelve rounds proving that a thumbprint, once pressed, does not need anyone's belief to survive contact.
